strengths: The paper addresses a relevant gap: evaluating memory in low-level robotic manipulation, complementing existing navigation and abstract memory benchmarks.

MIKASA-Robo offers substantial environment engineering: 32 variants across 12 task families, GPU-parallel simulation through ManiSkill3, multiple observation modes, and dense and sparse rewards. Appendix E provides useful task descriptions.
Oracle-state experiments provide evidence that the manipulation tasks are learnable. The strong LSTM advantage on RememberColor3 supplies an initial demonstration of sensitivity to memory mechanisms.
The experiments report three independent training runs, evaluation on 16 seeds per trained agent, and standard-error bands.
weaknesses: The central claim that the benchmark isolates memory is insufficiently supported. Comparing oracle-state observations with RGB+joints changes perception and state-estimation difficulty alongside memory requirements. Increasing color alternatives also changes visual discrimination and action selection. Matched visual-oracle controls, partially observed vector controls, and controlled retention-delay experiments are needed to attribute failures to memory.

Evaluation coverage is inadequate for the proposed scope. MIKASA-Base has no reported empirical evaluation. Figure 8 covers only 12 of the 32 robotic variants, with no RGB+joints results for the capacity and sequential families BunchOfColors, SeqOfColors, and ChainOfColors. Thus, two central taxonomy categories are not experimentally validated under the intended memory-testing configuration.

Only PPO-MLP and PPO-LSTM are evaluated, despite the paper motivating comparisons across diverse memory architectures. No attention-based or state-space baseline, frame-stacking control, or memory-horizon ablation establishes the suite's diagnostic value. Widespread near-zero sparse-reward results may primarily reflect exploration and optimization difficulties.

Figure 8 contains unexplained counterexamples to the memory interpretation: the memory-less MLP achieves high performance on ShellGameTouch and outperforms LSTM on InterceptSlow and RotateLenientPosNeg. These results warrant investigation of reactive strategies, repeated attempts, and information encoded through robot configuration before treating performance as a measure of internal memory.

The taxonomy is intuitive but lacks operational criteria or evidence of comprehensive coverage. Object and spatial memory overlap, while capacity is a dimension applicable to every category. The claimed minimal representative task selection is not supported by redundancy analysis or evidence that categories reveal distinct architectural strengths.

Reproducibility is materially incomplete. The manuscript omits network and visual-encoder specifications, PPO hyperparameters, recurrent training sequence lengths, and tuning procedures. The abstract's code-availability statement is unfinished and supplies no usable repository link; environment usage snippets do not reproduce the experiments.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Figures 6–7 show some oracle-state curves below perfect success, contradicting repeated assertions of consistently achieving 100% across all tasks. More fundamentally, oracle-state solvability does not establish that partially observed tasks are well-calibrated memory diagnostics or rule out benchmark-design problems.

These outcomes warrant investigation of reactive solutions, physical-state memory, and task shortcuts before asserting that performance measures internal memory capabilities.

Full-state solvability does not establish that partially observed task designs are well calibrated, and widespread sparse-reward failure does not distinguish memory limitations from exploration or credit-assignment failures.

The unified Gymnasium interface and extensive task descriptions could make the suite a useful community resource.

Comparing privileged vector-state policies with RGB+joints policies changes perception and information availability simultaneously. Evaluation is incomplete for a benchmark paper. MIKASA-Base has no reported experimental results, and the RGB+joints dense-reward comparison covers only 12 of 32 robotic variants, excluding the dedicated capacity and sequential task families. Only PPO-MLP and PPO-LSTM are evaluated, leaving the suite's ability to distinguish stronger memory architectures unestablished.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant gap: systematic evaluation of memory in robotic manipulation. MIKASA-Robo provides 32 task variants across 12 families, with configurable observations and dense or sparse rewards.
The ManiSkill3 implementation, Gymnasium interface, debugging tools, and reported release of expert datasets and checkpoints could provide useful infrastructure for subsequent research.
Evaluation spans online RL, offline learning, and VLA models. Table 6 provides results across all 32 tasks, while the appendices document task phases, success criteria, and reward components.

There is concrete evidence that memory helps on some tasks: RATE substantially outperforms memoryless offline baselines on ShellGameTouch and ShellGamePush, and PPO-LSTM outperforms PPO-MLP on RememberColor3. Full-state experiments also establish that the underlying manipulation tasks are solvable.
weaknesses: The central claim that performance degradation diagnoses memory limitations is insufficiently supported. Moving from oracle state to RGB observations simultaneously introduces perception and representation-learning challenges; increasing object counts also changes visual discrimination, target selection, and exploration. Full-state success does not isolate these factors. Matched RGB-plus-oracle controls, partially observed vector controls, and memory-reset or history-length ablations are needed.

The benchmark does not adequately establish that its tasks require internal memory or resist alternative strategies. Figure 9 shows strong memoryless performance on ShellGameTouch and InterceptMedium. Appendix H does not specify whether incorrect touches terminate the single-target selection tasks, leaving repeated candidate testing insufficiently addressed. The paper acknowledges action-chunking shortcuts but does not systematically test embodied memory, reactive policies, or cue removal.

The strongest claims rely heavily on failure results without sufficient diagnostic analysis. All five offline methods score zero on all nine capacity and sequential variants in Table 6. This leaves two proposed memory categories unable to distinguish the evaluated methods. Context-length sweeps, easier calibrated variants, partial-progress metrics, and a successful visual memory baseline would help establish whether these failures reflect memory demands or other training bottlenecks.

MIKASA-Base is presented as a major contribution but receives no empirical evaluation. The paper does not demonstrate that the unified suite improves architectural comparisons or supports the claimed attribution of memory-related failures. The four-category taxonomy is intuitive but overlapping: capacity applies to object, spatial, and sequential memory, and the claimed comprehensiveness is not established.

Baseline coverage is broad but insufficiently controlled for a memory benchmark. Online memory evaluation is largely limited to PPO-LSTM on selected tasks, without stronger recurrent or transformer-based online agents or simple frame-stacking comparisons. VLA experiments cover only five tasks with limited adaptation, so their failures do not establish general limitations of VLA memory.

Important experimental details and reporting inconsistencies limit reproducibility from the manuscript. Architecture sizes, recurrent training horizons, transformer context lengths, optimization settings, and tuning budgets are largely absent. Appendix F describes three training runs evaluated on 16 seeds, whereas Appendix G states that every algorithm uses 100 evaluation episodes. Appendix B describes sparse-reward oracle training, while Appendix F documents dense-reward oracle training. These protocols need clarification.

strengths: Addresses a relevant gap: evaluating memory in robotic manipulation beyond navigation and abstract puzzles. The 32 task variants across 12 families constitute a potentially useful research resource.

The ManiSkill3 implementation supports GPU parallelization, multiple observation modes, and dense/sparse rewards. The reported release of expert trajectories, checkpoints, and collection scripts strengthens its practical value.

Evaluation spans online RL, offline learning, and VLA models. Some results provide concrete evidence of memory benefits: PPO-LSTM solves RememberColor3, and RATE substantially outperforms memoryless offline baselines on ShellGameTouch and ShellGamePush.
The appendix provides detailed task descriptions, success criteria, and per-task offline results, including unsuccessful outcomes.
weaknesses: The central claim that performance degradation diagnoses memory limitations is insufficiently supported. Comparing privileged-state agents against RGB agents changes perception and information availability simultaneously. State-mode solvability does not establish that visual failures arise from memory. Matched RGB-plus-oracle controls and partially observed vector controls are needed to separate memory, perception, control, and optimization.

Memory necessity and resistance to shortcuts are not adequately validated. Figure 9 shows strong memoryless SAC/TD-MPC2 performance on ShellGameTouch and InterceptMedium, while Section 6.4 explicitly identifies action-chunking shortcuts. The task descriptions do not consistently specify whether incorrect selections terminate an episode or whether agents can encode cues through early movements. These issues require controlled memory-ablation and shortcut tests before success can be interpreted as a measure of internal memory.

Difficulty changes often introduce confounds rather than selectively increasing memory demands. ShellGame variants change manipulation difficulty, interception variants change speed, and RememberColor variants increase visual alternatives while retaining a single target attribute. No systematic retention-delay or history-length sweep establishes what memory capability each difficulty level measures.

The evaluation has substantial floor effects: all five offline methods score zero on all nine capacity/sequential variants in Table 6. This establishes difficulty but provides little discrimination between memory mechanisms. Easier calibrated settings, partial-progress metrics, and stronger online memory baselines would make the benchmark more informative. Limited VLA adaptation also weakens the broad conclusions about VLA memory limitations.

MIKASA-Base is presented as a major contribution but receives no empirical baseline evaluation. The four-part taxonomy is intuitive rather than validated: capacity cuts across object, spatial, and sequential memory, and the paper does not demonstrate that category-level scores reveal distinct architectural capabilities. Claims of comprehensive coverage and precise failure attribution exceed the evidence.

Important experimental details remain unclear in the manuscript, including online/offline architecture sizes, sequence lengths, recurrent training procedures, tuning budgets, and training durations. Statistical reporting also needs reconciliation: Appendix F describes three training runs with 16 evaluation seeds, Appendix G describes 100 evaluation episodes for every algorithm, and Table 6 reports uncertainty across three runs. These ambiguities limit reproducibility and confidence in comparisons.

strengths: Addresses a relevant gap: evaluating memory in robotic manipulation beyond navigation and synthetic recall tasks. The 32 task variants across 12 families provide a potentially useful research resource.

The engineering contribution is substantial: Gymnasium-compatible interfaces, GPU-parallel simulation, multiple observation and reward modes, and reported datasets containing 1,000 successful trajectories per task.

Evaluation covers online RL, offline learning, and VLA models. There is concrete evidence of memory benefits on some tasks: RATE achieves 0.92 success on ShellGameTouch versus 0.28 for BC, and PPO-LSTM substantially outperforms PPO-MLP on RememberColor3.
weaknesses: The central claim that performance diagnoses memory capability is insufficiently validated. Comparing privileged vector-state policies with RGB policies changes perception and information availability simultaneously. Increasing color count also changes visual discrimination, target selection, and exploration difficulty. Matched RGB-plus-oracle controls, partially observed vector controls, and controlled recall-delay sweeps are needed to isolate memory.

Memory-free shortcuts remain unresolved. Figure 9 shows PPO-MLP approaching roughly 90% success on ShellGameTouch despite the three possible hidden-ball locations. The paper also identifies action-chunking shortcuts in OpenVLA. These findings require systematic investigation of embodied information storage, repeated guesses, and task termination rules before success can be interpreted as a measure of internal memory.

The hardest categories provide little diagnostic discrimination: all five offline baselines score exactly zero on all nine capacity and sequential tasks in Table 6. This establishes difficulty but does not identify its source. Partial-progress metrics, history-length ablations, stronger memory baselines, and successful memory-enabled reference policies would make these tasks substantially more informative.

MIKASA-Base is presented as a major contribution but has no reported empirical evaluation. The taxonomy is useful organizationally, yet capacity overlaps with object, spatial, and sequential memory, and its comprehensiveness is not established. Claims of universal coverage and precise attribution of failures exceed the evidence.

Baseline configuration is insufficiently documented in the manuscript, particularly memory context lengths, recurrent training details, visual encoders, optimization budgets, and tuning. These are essential for interpreting failures on delayed-recall tasks. VLA evaluation covers only five tasks with limited adaptation, including training only Octo's readout heads, so it cannot establish broad limitations of VLA memory.

Several reporting inconsistencies weaken reproducibility: Appendix F describes three training runs evaluated on 16 seeds, whereas Appendix G describes 100 evaluation episodes for every algorithm; some plots label the metric as return while the discussion interprets it as success rate. Dataset collection is described as using sparse rewards in Appendix B, while the demonstrated oracle training uses dense rewards. These protocols need reconciliation.
